question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app for a course portfolio project built with React, Firebase, and Python. I was mainly assisting on the project, and we ran into an issue where part of the app was not behaving the way we expected, even though it seemed like the basic setup was correct.

What made it difficult was that the problem wasn’t obvious at first. I helped by going through the app step by step with the team, checking the parts we had recently changed, and comparing what was happening in the app with what we expected. We also used the browser tools and looked at the Firebase side to narrow things down.

In the end, we were able to identify the source of the issue and get the app working again. It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me the value of staying patient, being methodical, and communicating clearly when something is not immediately easy to spot.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a mobile app built with React, Firebase, and Python, and we ran into a bug that was hard to track down because it only showed up in certain situations. I helped by reproducing the issue, checking different parts of the app with my teammate, and comparing what was happening with what we expected.

I mostly assisted by narrowing down where the problem might be and trying small fixes while keeping notes on what we had already ruled out. I also used Firebase logs and the app itself to help us understand when the issue was happening.

It took some patience, but we were able to identify the main cause and get the app working properly again. That experience taught me to stay organized, be methodical, and not jump to conclusions when debugging.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app for a course portfolio project built with React, Firebase, and Python. I was mainly assisting with the work, and we ran into a bug that was hard to trace because the app seemed to work in some cases but not in others.

What made it difficult was that the issue didn’t show up consistently, so at first it was hard to tell whether the problem was in the app itself or somewhere else in the setup. I helped by reproducing the issue a few times, checking the error messages, and comparing what was happening in the app with what we expected.

I also worked with the team to narrow it down step by step instead of changing too many things at once. Using the browser tools and Firebase logs helped us get a better idea of where the problem was coming from.

In the end, we were able to identify the cause and get the app working more reliably. It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me how important it is to stay patient, observe carefully, and debug in a structured way.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a mobile app built with React, Firebase, and Python, and I helped debug an issue that was making the app behave inconsistently for some users. At first, it wasn’t obvious where the problem was coming from because the app seemed to work fine in some cases but not in others.

My role was mostly to assist by reproducing the issue, checking logs, and comparing what was happening in different parts of the app. I worked with the rest of the team to narrow it down step by step instead of guessing. That helped us understand where the problem was showing up and what part of the project needed attention.

It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me how important it is to stay patient and methodical when something is hard to track down. In the end, we were able to get the app working more reliably, and I came away with a better understanding of how to debug as part of a team.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database-backed application that was getting noticeably slow once the dataset grew. My part was to improve the performance of the Python and SQL layer, and I owned that work end to end.

I started by profiling the application instead of guessing. In Python, I used `cProfile` and timing logs around the main request flow, and in the database I looked at the slowest queries with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`. That showed me two main issues: we were making repeated queries inside a loop, and one of the larger queries was scanning the whole table because it was filtering on an unindexed column.

I fixed it in a few steps. First, I rewrote the Python code to batch the lookups instead of calling the database once per row. Then I changed the SQL to use a single join and added an index on the column used most often in the `WHERE` clause. I also removed a couple of unnecessary `SELECT *` calls and only fetched the fields the page actually needed, which reduced the amount of data transferred.

After those changes, I reran the same test dataset and measured the result. The slow page went from about 4.8 seconds to 0.9 seconds on my machine, so it was roughly 5 times faster. I also reduced the number of database queries for that flow from 120 down to 8. For the final demo, the application loaded smoothly with the full sample dataset, and I was able to show the before-and-after profiling results clearly.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built with Python, a REST API, and SQL, and I personally owned the debugging and improvement of the data update flow. We were seeing inconsistent results when records were created and then immediately queried through the API, especially in cases where related rows had to be inserted in the same transaction.

I traced the issue by adding targeted logging, reproducing the bug with a few failing test cases, and then stepping through the request handlers and SQL queries. I found that one endpoint was committing too early, while another was reading from a stale connection state, so the API could return success even though part of the write had not fully persisted. I also noticed one SQL query was doing a full table scan because the filter column wasn’t indexed, which made the slower endpoints much worse as the dataset grew.

I fixed it by restructuring the Python service layer so the write operations used a single transaction boundary, moved the commit to the end of the service method, and added proper rollback handling on exceptions. I also tightened the REST response logic so the API only returned success after the database transaction completed. On the SQL side, I added an index on the lookup column and rewrote one query to avoid unnecessary joins in the common path.

After that, I added and updated tests for the failing cases: one for transaction rollback, one for create-then-read consistency, and one for the optimized query path. The result was that the failing integration tests passed, the slow endpoint response time dropped from about 400 ms to under 100 ms in local testing, and the API became much more reliable during repeated test runs.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built with Python, a REST API, SQL, and automated tests. I personally owned the debugging and improvement of the data retrieval layer when we started seeing inconsistent results from the API, especially on filtered queries and pagination.

I traced the issue by reproducing it with specific requests, then checking the SQL being generated and comparing it to the expected output. I found two main problems: one was an inefficient query pattern that was doing extra full-table scans, and the other was a bug in how we were handling optional filters, which sometimes produced incorrect WHERE clauses. I fixed this by refactoring the query builder to assemble parameters more safely, using prepared statements consistently, and restructuring the SQL so filters were only added when present. I also added an index on the most frequently queried column, which improved response time for the common lookup path.

After that, I wrote and updated tests for the API endpoints and the database layer to cover edge cases like empty filters, invalid IDs, and pagination boundaries. I verified the fix by running the test suite and comparing before-and-after request timings. The result was that the failing queries became stable, the API returned correct results for all the cases we tested, and the average response time for the main endpoint dropped by about 40% in our local benchmark.

question: Tell me about a project where deployment or environment setup was part of the work.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small Python REST API for managing tasks, and I was responsible for the deployment and environment setup side of it. The main challenge was that the app had to run consistently across different laptops and in our demo environment, so I owned the decision to make the setup reproducible instead of relying on manual steps.

I set up the project with a virtual environment, pinned dependencies in `requirements.txt`, and added a simple configuration approach using environment variables for things like the database path and debug mode. For the API itself, I used Python with REST endpoints for creating, listing, updating, and deleting records, and I connected it to SQL through a lightweight database layer. I also wrote tests for the API routes and the database operations so we could verify the app still worked after deployment changes.

On the deployment side, I created a Dockerfile and a `docker-compose` setup so the API and database could be started with one command. I ran into an issue where the app worked locally but failed in the container because the database initialization happened too late, so I changed the startup flow to run migrations and seed data before the API server came up. I also had to fix a mismatch between local and container environment variables, which I caught by comparing test results inside and outside Docker.

To verify everything, I ran the test suite both locally and in the container, then did a full end-to-end check by hitting the REST endpoints with sample requests and confirming the SQL records were created correctly. In the end, the setup time for the project dropped from about 15 minutes of manual steps to under 2 minutes with one command, and the final demo ran without deployment issues.

question: Tell me about a project where something did not work at first and what you learned.
answer:
In my NLP course project, I built a small text classification service in Python with a REST API and a SQL database for storing labeled examples and prediction history. I owned the API design and the model integration end to end, and one thing that did not work at first was my original approach to preprocessing and model input.

At first, I exposed the raw text directly to the model and only did very light cleaning. The model looked fine in local experiments, but when I connected it to the API and tested it with real sample inputs, the predictions were inconsistent and the accuracy dropped a lot compared to my notebook results. I traced it by adding tests around the preprocessing pipeline and comparing the training input with the request-time input. I found that the training script and the API were not using the exact same normalization steps: one path lowercased and removed punctuation, while the other kept mixed casing and extra whitespace. I also noticed that some empty or very short texts were slipping through and causing unstable predictions.

I fixed it by moving preprocessing into a shared Python module used by both training and the REST endpoint, so the same function handled tokenization, lowercasing, punctuation removal, and input validation in both places. I added unit tests for edge cases like empty strings, repeated spaces, and non-ASCII characters, plus an integration test that sent sample requests through the API and checked the stored SQL records and returned predictions. After that, the model behavior became consistent between training and production-like requests, and the validation accuracy on my test set improved from about 71% to 84%.

What I learned was that in ML-related software, the model is only one part of the system. If the preprocessing, API, and data storage are not aligned, the whole result can look broken even when the model itself is fine. Since then, I always try to make the data flow explicit, share code where it makes sense, and write tests around the boundaries between components.

question: Describe a project where you collaborated with others but had a clear personal contribution.
answer:
In my final-year portfolio project, I worked with two other students on a machine learning web app that predicted whether a customer was likely to churn. The overall project was collaborative, but I personally owned the backend prediction service and most of the debugging work around data flow and model integration.

My main responsibility was building the Python REST API that connected the trained model to the frontend. I used Flask to expose a `/predict` endpoint, validated incoming JSON, and made sure the request format matched the feature set the model expected. I also wrote the SQL queries to pull historical training data from our database and helped define the exact schema for the input features so we could keep training and inference consistent.

A big part of my contribution was debugging an issue where the model looked accurate offline, but the API was returning inconsistent predictions in the app. I traced it to a mismatch between the training pipeline and the live request payload: one-hot encoded columns were being generated in a different order, and a few numeric fields were coming through as strings. I fixed that by centralizing the preprocessing logic in Python, adding explicit type conversion and feature ordering before inference, and then writing tests to cover both valid and invalid payloads.

I also added unit tests for the API endpoints and a few integration tests to verify that a sample request returned the expected response shape and status code. After the fix, our prediction endpoint became stable, and we were able to demo the full flow end to end without errors. As a result, the project went from failing on several test cases to passing all of our API and preprocessing tests, and the final demo handled real sample inputs reliably.

question: Tell me about a project where testing changed how you built the feature.
answer:
In my course portfolio project, I built a small testing framework in Python for a REST API backed by SQL, and testing changed the feature design pretty early. I originally planned to have the API return a single generic response for all validation errors, but when I started writing tests, I realized that would make both debugging and automation harder.

I owned the implementation of the test suite, so I wrote integration tests with `pytest` that covered the main API flows: creating records, updating them, handling duplicate data, and checking database state directly with SQL after each request. One test exposed a problem where the API returned `200 OK` even when the payload was missing a required field, because the route handler was only checking the request body loosely and the SQL insert was failing later. That made me redesign the endpoint so validation happened before any database call, and I added explicit `400` responses with field-level error messages.

I also changed the response structure based on the tests. Instead of one generic error string, I made the API return a consistent JSON format like `{"error": "...", "field": "..."}` so the tests could assert exact behavior and future cases would be easier to extend. After that, I added setup and teardown logic in the framework to seed test data and clean the database between runs, which reduced flaky failures caused by leftover rows.

The measurable result was that the suite went from catching only basic happy-path issues to covering both API and database behavior across 15+ test cases, and it exposed two real bugs before I considered the feature done. It also made the final implementation more predictable, because I was designing the endpoint around what the tests needed to verify rather than patching behavior afterward.

question: Describe a project where you collaborated with others but had a clear personal contribution.
answer:
In my course project, I worked on a small machine learning system that predicted whether a customer support ticket should be escalated. The team had three people, and my main responsibility was the Python backend that exposed the model through a REST API and handled the data flow from SQL to prediction.

My clearest personal contribution was debugging a problem where the model looked accurate in training, but the API predictions were inconsistent in testing. I traced it down by checking the full path end to end: the SQL query, the feature preprocessing, and the request payload sent to the endpoint. I found that one of the categorical fields was being encoded differently in the API than in the training notebook, so the model was receiving mismatched feature values. I fixed that by moving the preprocessing into a shared Python pipeline used both during training and inference, and I added validation so the API would reject incomplete or malformed requests with a clear error message.

I also wrote unit tests for the preprocessing functions and API tests for the `/predict` endpoint using sample JSON payloads. After the fix, the test accuracy in the project stayed stable at about 87%, and the API returned consistent predictions across repeated runs. The final demo worked reliably, and our team was able to show a complete flow from SQL data retrieval to model inference through the REST API.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database-backed system with a Python REST API and SQL layer, and I personally owned a bug fix that improved both reliability and performance. We were seeing inconsistent results when users created and updated records through the API, and some endpoints were also slower than expected.

I started by reproducing the issue locally with the test data and tracing the request flow from the REST endpoint down to the SQL queries. I found two main problems: first, one endpoint was doing multiple separate queries inside a loop instead of using a single parameterized query, which caused unnecessary round trips to the database. Second, a few update paths were not handling transaction boundaries correctly, so partial writes could happen if one step failed.

I fixed this by refactoring the Python service layer to use a single transaction for each write operation and by replacing the repeated queries with a more efficient SQL join and batch fetch. I also tightened the input validation in the API so invalid payloads were rejected earlier, before hitting the database. After that, I added and updated unit tests and integration tests to cover the failure cases I had found, including rollback behavior and duplicate record handling.

To verify the improvement, I compared the endpoint behavior before and after the change. The slowest request path went from about 180 ms to around 70 ms in my local test environment, and the flaky write failures stopped showing up in the test suite. More importantly, the API became consistent under error conditions, and the tests gave us confidence that the fix would hold up.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In my portfolio project, I built a Python REST API for managing course data, and one technical problem I solved was how to keep the API fast and consistent when several endpoints needed the same related data from SQL.

At first, I had endpoints like `GET /courses`, `GET /courses/{id}`, and `GET /students/{id}/courses`, and I was doing separate SQL queries inside each route handler. That worked, but I noticed two issues during testing: response times were getting slower as the data grew, and some endpoints were returning slightly different shapes of data because each handler was assembling the response a bit differently.

I took ownership of that part of the API and redesigned it so the database layer handled the shared query logic. I created a small repository/service layer in Python that used parameterized SQL queries and joins to fetch the exact data each endpoint needed in one query instead of multiple round trips. For example, for the course detail endpoint, I changed it from querying the course first and then looping to fetch related records, to a single query with joins and grouping in Python after the fetch. I also standardized the response schema in one place so all endpoints returned the same field names and nested structure.

While doing that, I ran into a bug where duplicate rows were appearing because of the join on a one-to-many relationship. I debugged it by printing the raw SQL results and comparing them to the expected objects, then fixed it by deduplicating on the course ID and building the nested list explicitly in the service layer. I added tests for the repository functions and API endpoints using pytest, including cases for empty results, missing IDs, and duplicate-related rows. I also added assertions on the exact JSON structure so I could catch regressions if the response shape changed.

The result was that the API became more predictable and easier to maintain, and the slowest endpoint went from about 300 ms to around 120 ms in my local testing with seeded data. More importantly, I had a cleaner design that made the rest of the project easier to extend.

question: Tell me about a project where something did not work at first and what you learned.
answer:
In one of my NLP course projects, I built a small text classification service in Python with a REST API and a SQL database to store predictions and feedback. I owned the backend implementation end to end, including the API endpoints, the database schema, and the test suite.

What didn’t work at first was the prediction flow. The model was returning reasonable results in my notebook, but when I connected it to the API, the output was inconsistent and sometimes the same input produced different labels. I first thought it was a problem with the model itself, but after tracing the request through the code, I found two issues: the text preprocessing in the API was not identical to the preprocessing used during training, and I was also reloading the model on every request, which made debugging harder and slowed the endpoint down.

I fixed it by extracting the preprocessing into a shared Python function used by both training and inference, so tokenization and normalization were consistent. I also changed the API to load the model once at startup instead of inside the request handler. After that, I added tests for the preprocessing function, the prediction endpoint, and a few database write cases to make sure the stored results matched the API response.

The result was that the endpoint became stable, response time improved noticeably, and the tests caught a couple of edge cases with empty input and punctuation-heavy text before demo day. The main thing I learned was to verify the full path from training to production code, not just the model in isolation, and to use tests early when there are multiple moving parts like NLP, APIs, and SQL.

question: Tell me about a project where testing changed how you built the feature.
answer:
In my course portfolio project, I built a small testing framework in Python for a REST API backed by SQL, and testing changed the feature design pretty early for me.

I originally planned to write the API tests as simple end-to-end checks that hit the real database every time. After I started writing the first test cases, I realized that approach made the suite slow and flaky because the same data was being reused across tests, and failures were hard to debug when one test polluted the next. So I changed the design before I went too far.

I refactored the framework to create test data through setup fixtures and to clean up records after each run. I also added SQL assertions for the database state, not just API response checks, so I could verify both the HTTP layer and the persistence layer. For example, after a `POST /users` request, I would assert the `201` response, then query the database directly to confirm the row was inserted with the expected fields and timestamps. That helped me catch a bug where the API returned success, but one column was being saved as `NULL` because of a mapping issue in the request handler.

I personally owned the test design, the Python test code, and the SQL verification queries. I used the failing tests to guide the implementation, especially around idempotent setup and teardown. Once I switched to isolated test data and database assertions, the suite became much more reliable.

The result was that I got the full test run down from about 12 minutes to 4 minutes, and I increased coverage of the main API flows from roughly 60% to 90%. More importantly, the tests caught two data-mapping bugs before I considered the feature done, so testing directly shaped how I built the final version.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course portfolio project, I worked on a small database system built with Python, a REST API, and SQL. I personally owned the part where I improved how the application handled repeated reads and writes, because the first version was getting slow and inconsistent once we started testing it with more realistic data.

My main change was to redesign a few API flows so they used clearer SQL transactions and fewer round trips to the database. For example, one endpoint was doing multiple separate queries to check whether a record existed, insert it, and then fetch the result. I changed that to use a single transaction with parameterized SQL and a returning query where possible, which reduced the chance of race conditions and made the code easier to reason about. I also added input validation in the REST layer so bad requests were rejected before hitting the database.

I verified the changes with tests at a few levels. I wrote unit tests for the Python service logic, API tests for the endpoints, and SQL-focused tests for edge cases like duplicate keys, missing fields, and rollback behavior when one statement failed. While debugging, I found one issue where a test was passing locally but failing in CI because the database state was not being reset between runs, so I fixed the test setup to create and tear down a clean schema for each test case.

The result was that the API became more reliable and noticeably faster under the project’s test workload. In our benchmark script, the updated endpoint reduced average response time by about 35%, and the test suite became stable enough to run consistently in CI without flaky failures.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
In my team course project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool that pulled data from CSV files and generated scheduled reports with Python and cron. My specific task was to build the part that cleaned the incoming CSV data and produced a daily summary file that the rest of the tool could use.

The main constraint was time and reliability. We only had a short window to get the demo working, and the CSV files were not always consistent — some rows had missing values, extra spaces, or slightly different column order. I had to make sure the report generation would still run automatically without breaking.

I handled that by writing a Python script that validated the required columns, normalized the data, and skipped or flagged bad rows instead of stopping the whole job. I also added logging so we could see exactly what was rejected and why. Then I set up a cron job to run the script every morning and output a clean summary CSV for the dashboard.

The measurable result was that before this, the team was manually fixing the input files and it was taking about 20 to 30 minutes each day. After my script was in place, the report ran automatically in under 2 minutes, and our final demo used the scheduled output successfully without any manual cleanup.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app for a course project using React and Firebase. I was helping with the front-end and some of the data flow, and we ran into a bug where certain user actions were not saving correctly, but only sometimes. That made it hard to track down because it didn’t happen every time.

I helped by testing different steps in the app, checking the browser console, and comparing when the issue happened versus when it worked. We eventually found that the problem was related to how the app was handling the data before sending it to Firebase. I worked with the team to adjust that part and re-test it several times.

It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me how important it is to debug carefully and not assume the first thing you see is the real cause. In the end, we got the issue resolved and the app was working more reliably.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app built with React and Firebase for a course project. We ran into an issue where the app would sometimes not show the latest data after a user made an update, and at first it wasn’t obvious whether the problem was in the frontend or with Firebase.

I helped by testing different parts of the flow and comparing what was happening in the app with what was actually being saved in Firebase. I also worked with my team to narrow it down by checking the timing of the data fetches and looking at where the state was being updated. It took a bit of trial and error, but that helped us understand that the app wasn’t always refreshing at the right time.

What I learned from that experience was to debug step by step instead of guessing, and to verify each part of the process separately. In the end, we were able to improve the behavior of the app and make it more reliable.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app built with React and Firebase for a course project. I helped with the debugging when we started seeing an issue where some user data wasn’t showing up correctly after login.

At first, it wasn’t obvious what was wrong because the app seemed to work for some users but not others. I assisted by checking the flow step by step, looking at the login process, the data being sent and received, and comparing what was happening in the app with what we expected. I also worked with the rest of the team to narrow down whether the problem was in the front end or in Firebase.

What made it difficult was that the issue didn’t happen every time, so we had to test it a few different ways and be patient while tracing it. In the end, we found the cause and made a fix that improved the app’s reliability. It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me how important it is to debug carefully and not assume the first thing you see is the real problem.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.

It was a good learning experience because it showed me how important it is to test edge cases and to debug step by step instead of assuming the first thing you see is the root cause. In the end, we were able to improve the behavior and make the app more reliable.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app built with React and Firebase for a course project. I helped out with debugging when we started seeing an issue where some user data wasn’t showing up correctly after login.

My role was mostly to assist by testing different parts of the app, checking the flow from the frontend to Firebase, and helping narrow down where the problem was happening. At first, it wasn’t obvious whether the issue was in the UI or in how the data was being saved and loaded, so I went step by step and compared what I expected to happen with what was actually happening.

What helped most was staying organized and testing one change at a time. I also asked questions when I got stuck, which helped me understand the problem better instead of guessing. In the end, we were able to identify the issue and get the app working more reliably.

That project taught me that debugging is often about being patient, breaking the problem down, and not assuming the first thing you see is the real cause.

question: Tell me about a project where something did not work at first and what you learned.
answer:
In a course project, I built a small NLP service in Python that took text, classified it, and exposed the result through a REST API backed by SQL. I owned the API design and the integration between the model, the database, and the tests.

At first, my design did not work well because I was storing the raw text and the prediction in the same request flow, and the endpoint was timing out whenever the input was a bit larger. I also had a bug where the same text could be processed twice if the client retried the request, which created duplicate rows in the database. I initially assumed the issue was in the model, but after adding logging and running the endpoint locally with test payloads, I found the bottleneck was actually the synchronous processing inside the API layer.

I fixed it by separating the request validation, text preprocessing, and prediction steps more clearly. I also added a unique request hash in SQL so repeated submissions would be detected instead of inserted again. On the testing side, I wrote unit tests for the preprocessing function, API tests for status codes and duplicate handling, and a few integration tests that hit the endpoint with sample texts and checked the database state afterward.

After that change, the endpoint response time for normal requests dropped from around 2–3 seconds to under 500 ms in my local tests, and the duplicate-record issue was eliminated in the test suite. What I learned was that a design can look fine on paper, but for NLP systems the API boundary, data flow, and idempotency matter just as much as the model itself. I also learned to debug by isolating each layer instead of assuming the first thing I built was the problem.

question: Tell me about a project where something did not work at first and what you learned.
answer:
In my NLP course project, I was building a text classification model in Python with scikit-learn to label short student feedback into categories like “content,” “organization,” and “clarity.” My part was to design the preprocessing and validation approach, because at first our model looked much better on the training data than it did on new examples.

Initially, I used a very simple setup: lowercasing, removing punctuation, and then a TF-IDF vectorizer with a logistic regression classifier. On the training set, the accuracy was around 92%, so I thought we were in good shape. But when I tested it on a held-out validation set, performance dropped to about 68%, and the model was especially bad at the smaller classes. That was the first sign that something in the design was off, not just the model itself.

I dug into the error cases and realized two things. First, I had been tuning the model while looking too much at the training results, which made me overestimate how well it generalized. Second, our validation split was not representative enough because the classes were imbalanced. I changed the workflow so we used a proper train/validation split with stratification, and I compared several options using the validation set instead of the training score. I also added n-grams to the TF-IDF features and set `class_weight='balanced'` in logistic regression. That helped the model pay more attention to the smaller labels.

After those changes, validation accuracy improved from 68% to 81%, and macro F1 went up by about 14 points. More importantly, the model stopped missing the minority categories as often, which made the final demo much more convincing. The main thing I learned was that a design decision can look fine on paper, but if you don’t validate it properly, you can end up optimizing for the wrong thing. Since then, I’ve been much more careful about using a validation set early and checking class balance before trusting any metric.

One project I worked on was a React web app for a course project. It was basically a small app where users could view different pieces of content and interact with the interface in a simple way. I used React and JavaScript for most of it, and I helped with building some of the components and making sure the pages worked together.

I was more of a support role on the project, so I assisted with things like setting up parts of the UI, fixing small bugs, and helping connect different pieces of the app. It was a good experience for me because I got to see how a project comes together from start to finish, and I learned a lot about working with React in a real project setting.

Overall, it went pretty well and helped me get more comfortable with front-end development and working with a team.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app for a course project. It was basically a small front-end app where users could view different pages and interact with some simple features, and I used React and JavaScript for most of it. I helped out with building a few components and connecting the UI together, so I wasn’t doing everything on my own, but I did get to work through a lot of the setup and logic with the team.

What I learned most from it was how to break a bigger task into smaller pieces and how to make components work together more cleanly. I also got more comfortable with debugging and figuring out why something wasn’t rendering the way I expected. Overall, it was a good experience because it gave me a better understanding of how React projects are put together, and the final app came out pretty well.

Overall, it helped me get more confident with React and gave me a better idea of how to work on a team and keep improving as I go.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app for a course project. It was basically a small app where users could view different pages and interact with some simple features, and I used JavaScript and React for most of it. I helped with building a few of the components and connecting the pieces together so the app would work smoothly.

I wasn’t the main person driving everything, but I assisted with things like setting up parts of the UI, handling some basic state, and fixing bugs when things didn’t behave the way we expected. It was a good experience because I got to see how a React project comes together and how important it is to keep the code organized even in a smaller project.

Overall, it helped me get more comfortable with React and working on a team, and I learned a lot from just trying things out and debugging along the way.
